During the height of the US-China trade war under Donald Trump, with tariffs seemingly rising every week, companies like Logitech responded with significant price hikes on their US products.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled these tariffs unlawful, requiring refunds to manufacturers. Yet no company has been seen passing those refunds on to consumers, and a class-action lawsuit is now seeking to address this...

The Trump tariff saga

Last year, Trump seized on the US trade deficit with China, apparently believing that imposing higher tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to bring manufacturing back to the US.

In reality, this was never going to happen. The country simply does not have the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise, or cheap workforce required to support production at the scale of major brands.

Trump consistently claimed China would pay the tariffs, but the reality is that the US companies importing the finished Chinese goods paid them, then passed these additional costs on to consumers through price hikes. At the peak of this debacle, tariff rates reached as high as 145%.

Take Logitech as an example. The company raised prices on around half its products by up to 25%.

Consumers deserve refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and ordered refunds to be paid to US companies. That refund process is currently underway.

The problem is that the costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, and there is currently no indication that any affected company plans to refund customers.

Law firm CPM has filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech over this, seeking refunds for consumers who paid higher prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's take

The principle here is indisputable. The companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra costs on to consumers, and the government is now refunding the companies. Morally, they should refund the corresponding portion of the purchase price to consumers who bought products during this period.

However, putting this into practice would be enormously challenging. Logitech would need to work through its vast network of third-party retailers to identify every transaction, track what price each consumer paid, and calculate what proportion of that constituted tariff costs.

If this lawsuit succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent – though as we always note, the main winners in class-action lawsuits tend to be the lawyers, with consumers typically receiving very small payouts.
